Christ is in us and is our head, the men’s head. He is that crown of glory to us, because our mind is stayed on his mind and our desires are unto him. Whatever he wants to accomplish, we want to accomplish, and what he wants to accomplish is what his head, God, wants him to accomplish. So when it says in that day the Lord of hosts will be for a crown of glory, that is the crown we wear now in our minds.

“For Zion’s sake will I not hold my peace, and for Jerusalem’s sake I will not rest, until the righteousness thereof go forth as brightness, and the salvation thereof as a lamp that burneth. And the Gentiles shall see thy righteousness”: they’re going to see our righteousness, “and all kings thy glory.”

“And thou shalt be called by a new name, which the mouth of the Lord shall name.” That’s how you know this is a different time: we’ll be called by a new name that the mouth of the Lord will name. So when we read in Isaiah 28 about ‘in that day’, it’s talking about now, in our redemption: that we retain Christ in our mind and in our spirits, that we’re not reprobates, that he’s our head, the crown that we wear.

Keep reading: “Thou shalt also be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a royal diadem in the hand of thy God.” We in his hand are going to be his glory. Just like the women will not have any glory till the men get theirs, the men cannot have glory until Christ gets his. And when all things are brought to his feet, Christ is going to bring that to his head’s feet, and all that’s promised will be fulfilled.

sense.text: “The wisdom of a learned man cometh by opportunity of leisure.” If you want to get wisdom and strengthen yourself in wisdom, you have to make the time to have that leisure, because we all have responsibilities, and on top of that there are the masturbatory substitutes that prevent you from increasing in wisdom. “And he that hath little business shall become wise.”

“How can he get wisdom that holdeth the plough”, “that driveth oxen, and is occupied in their labours”? It says it in a right way for that time, because they didn’t have video games and movies and all this other stuff to distract you back then. But you could throw that in the mix now too, because that’s the bane of a lot of brothers in increasing in growth and understanding.
Again, different ways to strengthen ourselves. “Give not over thy mind to heaviness”: don’t give your mind to heaviness. “And afflict not thyself in thine own counsel.”
“The gladness of the heart is the life of man, and the joyfulness of a man prolongeth his days.”

“Love thine own soul”: love your own soul and do it no harm. “Comfort thy heart, remove sorrow far from thee”: nobody cares you’re going through it; that’s life, time and chance is for all of us. “For sorrow hath killed many, and there is no profit therein.”

“Envy and wrath shorten the life, and carefulness bringeth age before the time. A cheerful and good heart will have a care of his meat and diet.” So you have psychological health, and then you have physical health.

“Eat as it becometh a man, those things which are set before thee”, “lest thou be hated. Leave off first for manners’ sake; and be not unsatiable, lest thou offend.” It goes into how we should be when it comes to food, as well as table manners. All these things strengthen us.

“When thou sittest among many, reach not thine hand out first of all. A very little is sufficient for a man well nurtured”: you just eat healthy foods; that’s what well nurtured is, in the proper moderation.

“Sound sleep cometh of moderate eating: he riseth early, and his wits are with him: but the pain of watching, and choler, and pangs of the belly, are with an unsatiable man.”

You would think, damn, why jump into diet after all this wisdom stuff in the head? Remember: your thoughts become words, words become actions, then habits, and then it becomes your character. Notice it didn’t say unsatiable appetite; it said unsatiable man. If you can’t display your discipline in your fatness and in your drunkenness, you might be an alcoholic, one of those high-functioning ones, always drinking on the weekends or at home, thinking you don’t have an alcohol problem because you’re not sloppy drunk all the time. You’re unsatiable.

There’s a connection between the stomach and the character. They call your digestive system the second brain now, and they say the way you care for it affects everything else; it’s the key to a lot of diseases and longevity. If you’re an unsatiable person in your eating, in your alcohol, whatever it is that you do, you will have that as your actions.

precepts.why:
This is why it says, “Go not after thy lusts, but refrain thyself from thine appetites.” Don’t be unsatiable. It calls them appetites; it likens lust to food.

So if you can’t be faithful in little, which is your diet and caring for yourself, how do you think you’re such a disciplined person, so on fire in this walk? You don’t have to have a six-pack, but it sure will help if you build yourself a good foundation in your fitness routine. It’ll carry over into everything else.

sense.text: ‘Good’: when problems come, you have the opportunity to learn, you have the opportunity to figure out a solution. “My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations”: good. Remember Paul sought thrice for it to be removed from him, and was told ‘my grace is sufficient for thee.’ Count it all joy when you fall into divers temptations: it’s an opportunity to get strong.

“Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience. But let patience have her perfect work”: let it do what it’s supposed to do. Take the opportunity, learn something, get better, “that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.” Let it be perfect: give it the time to perfect in you, and meditate on it.

“But God hath revealed them unto us by his Spirit: for the Spirit searcheth all things, yea, the deep things of God.” “Even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.” So you have to focus on that spirit of God and stay in that mindset. Let that crown, that head, be your thoughts.

“Now we have received, not the spirit of the world, but the spirit which is of God; that we might know the things that are freely given to us of God”: these are steps for us to focus on that mind of Christ.
“Which things also we speak, not in the words which man’s wisdom teacheth”: we speak as the oracles of God, “but which the Holy Ghost teacheth; comparing spiritual things with spiritual.”

“But the natural man receiveth not the things of the Spirit of God.” We all are the natural man, but we’re also the spiritual man; there is a duality in us. That’s how we live and move: we’re in these fleshly bodies, and this is why we have to be in control. It’s like jumping into one of those exoskeletons they show in movies and letting it control things. It’s not supposed to be that way. You steer this; you run this.

“For they are foolishness unto him: neither can he know them, because they are spiritually discerned.” We must work on our spiritual discernment, which only comes through the mind of Christ.

“But he that is spiritual judgeth all things, yet he himself is judged of no man.” You’re not going to be judged of any man, because you’re going to judge those things in your mind before they become words, actions and habits. You’re getting it right in your head, comparing spiritual to spiritual, so nobody’s going to have to tell you, damn, you messed up and you should have known better. You kill it in your head.

“For who hath known the mind of the Lord, that he may instruct him?” Nobody has known the mind of the Lord that he may instruct him, but he instructed one. “But we have the mind of Christ”: that crown of glory that’s on our head.

“The elders which are among you I exhort, who am also an elder, and a witness of the sufferings of Christ, and also a partaker of the glory that shall be revealed.” When we hear elders, I’m thinking of the deacons that are above me, the Bishops that are above me. You’re thinking elders and it might be the soldier that’s above you or the officer that’s above you. But all of us fall into this in some form.

“Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind.” We have to focus on building each other up. Of a ready mind: keep thy heart with all diligence, lift up the weak hands and the feeble knees. Get your eye right.
“Neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock”: you show them in your actions.

“And when the chief Shepherd shall appear”, when Christ appears, “ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away.” We have that crown of glory now in retaining that spirit of Christ in us, but when he arrives, in that day, that crown of glory will not fade away. We won’t have to fight to keep that crown of glory anymore, if you show that you can fight for it now and hold on to it now.
